item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports separating interests across temporal scales. [MIMAR-SRec (AAAI 2026)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/38489) learns intent representations from different contextual windows, with prototype and cross-user contrastive alignment. [MARS (2026 preprint)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07505) maintains recurrent memories with different half-lives and selectively routes among them; its authors report larger gains after behavioral shifts. [IBLSRec (2025)](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10820829/) combines personalized preferences, intent guidance, and stable item relationships to address sparsity, although it treats short-term item relationships as noise—an assumption that may suppress genuine immediate needs.\n\nFor sparse histories, [ICSRec (WSDM 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.14318) constructs subsequences and transfers supervision across sequences sharing a target item, learning coarse and fine intent structure without explicit intent labels. Explicit change-point modeling is less prominent in these recent results; an earlier [HMM approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.00272) directly detects preference changes from interaction sequences. A practical synthesis, rather than an established result: retain a slow preference state and a fast intent state, then learn a soft reset or mixing gate from observed time gaps and disagreement between recent embeddings and historical state. Multiple decay rates offer a lightweight alternative to fixed windows; shared intent prototypes could provide statistical support when individual histories are short. These are architectural hypotheses requiring validation on the four-category benchmark, not evidence of improved HR@10 there."}
